posts.name: Kaivax
posts.cooked:
We’ve recently completed a round of actions taken against accounts that were found to have participated in spending real money on gold provided by a third party (RMT). Some of the accounts actioned purchased the illicit gold and had the seller deliver it to a different player who provided a service to the purchaser, such as a raid carry.

Please be reminded that gold received from an intermediate player has an extremely high likelihood of being illicit gold that was part of an RMT. To avoid actions such as account suspension and the removal of illicit gold, players should always directly transfer gold from the player buying the carry (or other activity) to the player providing the carry.

Guilds that provide carries to players, who pay for them with gold that comes from an intermediate, are at risk of seeing that gold removed by Blizzard.

Thank you very much!

posts.name: Marco
posts.cooked:
I think it’s time devs looked at the reasons people want to boost in-game. My take is that boosting boils down to a few reasons:

  • “I don’t feel I’m good enough, or others don’t think I am, and FOMO.”

  • “I don’t have a lot of time to play.”

  • “I really do not want to boost another alt, farm all those crests, etc.”

Now, you can’t always fix reasons one and two, but the third one can be fixed almost overnight (I say overnight, but it’s probably next season). This could be done by making crests account-wide once they unlock, or allowing your alts to gain crests once your main is capped for the week. Hell, I’d even argue it could soften point two.

Say you have X main, and you’re capping out Mythic crests each week. You’re still doing keys because you like them (or hate yourself, whatever), and you can see your toon getting Hero crests, Champion crests, Veteran… Mar… you get it.

Having the option to send those Mythic crests to alts Y and Z would probably incentivise players to pick up alts. What sounds better for engagement?

Having an alt geared within 5–10 ilvls of your main fairly quickly, spending weeks catching up, or not bothering and going to play another game? I know commercially you don’t want the last choice, and I can confidently suggest option two is dull for players.

It’s dull because you rely on the goodwill of your guild, friends, or community. It’s dull because you spend time being rejected from keys you’re capable of doing. Or you buy boosts and get the gear, score, and crests in the most effective way. Which would you pick? Which would most of the player base pick?

You can further incentivise players by removing vault-looted items from bonus rolls. This season has rendered the game into bonus-roll resets for the most part. Don’t get me wrong: bonus rolls in week two, with the opportunity to roll higher-track loot (or 6/6 Mythic after a Mythic kill), feel great. The power spikes are fun, the kill feels worth it, but I wonder how many people opened the vault after their first Ula’tec kill, saw an item they wanted, and couldn’t take it in case they bonus-rolled it the week after? How crap, frankly, is that?

Boosting has its place in WoW… to a point. Right now, your game design is pushing people to buy boosts, boosters to boost alts, and everyone and his dog to try to boost for a steady gold stream.

Pull the ripcord. Open crests up to alts. Increase the discount on alts to further incentivise players to try a new class, a new role, without completely needing to start from scratch.

If the choice is between allowing those who are already playing to have a bit more fun, but play a week or two less because they have better loot options and alts are easier to get into shape, or having the game run into the ground by boosting and the advertising spam that goes with it, go with the first option. I think we’re already on the path to the latter.

I hope you enjoyed my mini TED Talk. I also hope others throw some ideas in, critique this, expand on it, whatever.

Technically speaking, I have a hard time understanding why this is against the rules.

If (A) spends money and buys some gold from (B) on a website, and (B) delivers the gold to (C) in the game, and (C) provides a boost to (A) in a raid, what exactly has (A) done that violates the rules?

(B) is a gold-seller. Take action against his account, fine.

(C) receives gold from (B) and provides a raid boost for (A). Why is the action of (C) against the rules?

So in summary: I don’t understand this. You’re outlining some action you’ve taken, but where’s the policy? Link your damn policy! “Gold Transactions Must Be Direct”. Okay, link the policy where it says so explicitly.
You wrote a bunch of words that is the equivalent of a story text. You wrote a story about something you’ve done as a company. Okay, cool, whatever. Link your policy that outlines in detail what is allowed and isn’t allowed as it pertains to gold-buying, trading, and player services.
Creating these random posts, of which this is just the latest among many, is ridiculous.

Stop with the story writing and just link your damn policy.

You accept all these things when you install the game, they do not need a reason to ban you if they want to or think that you RMT etc.

First of all, I haven’t actually accepted anything related to this. As I said in my initial post – where’s the policy? Where are the specific policies pertaining to these matters written? Blizzard writing a random forum post doesn’t constitute in-game policy that anyone can navigate in with regards to their own gameplay experience. Nothing in Blizzard’s post actually says anything about what players are allowed to do and what they aren’t allowed to do.

Secondly, it is true that Blizzard reserves the right to take action against anyone for any reason whatsoever – and even for no reason at all. But the point of Blizzard’s post is surely not to establish themselves as an evil overlord who acts without reason or cause with regards to the playerbase. Having written policy that specifies what’s allowed and what’s not allowed, lets Blizzard ban players for a reason as opposed to no reason. And it allows them to ban players because they know they’ve done something that isn’t allowed, as opposed to banning them because they think or feel they’ve done something that isn’t to their liking.

Ergo, they should outline the in-game policy regarding these areas, so players know what’s up and down.
I don’t think anyone has a problem accepting Blizzard’s in-game policies – they just need to know what they are. And that would require that Blizzard actually writes them in the first place. Which they don’t seem to have gotten around to, hence why we get these ridiculous posts instead.

Blizzard are guessing what they can’t prove, and sometimes they guess wrong.
